James Joyce is so difficult because he was remarkably intelligent and had an unusually large vocabulary which he used to its fullest extent.

He's held to be a "great author" by different people for different reasons. Personally, I count him as a "great author" because I too possess an unusually large vocabulary, so I have enough familiarity with the language to appreciate the care with which he chose words in order to craft his stories. Others grant him less acclaim, all the way down to the assertion that he was a terrible author, generally because they believe that his use of language obscured his storytelling. I can't fault them for that - there are many much better storytellers out there. Nonetheless, as a person who appreciates the careful and imaginative use of an extensive vocabulary in order to convey interesting nuances of otherwise mundane things, I appreciate the notable skill with which Joyce did exactly that.

Sometimes complexity cannot be reduced for understanding by lesser minds without losing meaning. Take, for example, any part of Stephen Hawking's groundbreaking work. Unless you're a physicist or a mathematician, you don't stand a snowball's chance in hell of understanding a single one of his equations, much less its meaning in the larger whole.

That's James Joyce. You've got to be able to work language like a pro to get a glimpse of his meaning. For the rest, there's Cliff Notes.
